# The 12 Futures of AI

## A beginner’s guide to the most important decision humanity has ever faced, and why the ending is still ours to write.

--

Listen

Share

Based on Max Tegmark’s Life 3.0

You have probably heard someone say that AI is going to change everything. Maybe you nodded politely and went back to your coffee. Fair enough. But here is the thing: MIT professor Max Tegmark, one of the world’s most respected physicists, has mapped out exactly what “everything” might look like, and the range of possibilities is wider than almost anyone imagines.

Some futures look like paradise. Others look like paradise until you try to leave. And a few are genuinely terrifying. But the most important thing Tegmark wants you to know is this: none of these futures are inevitable. We get to choose. Or rather, if we do not choose, someone will choose for us.

Let’s take a walk through the 12 possible worlds that might be waiting for us, starting with the familiar and ending with the truly mind-bending.

> First, a Quick Vocabulary Lesson: Before we dive in, one term you will keep hearing is AGI, short for Artificial General Intelligence. Unlike the AI assistants you use today, which are good at specific tasks, AGI would be capable of doing anything a human mind can do, and then some. Think less “smart autocomplete” and more “a new kind of mind.” That is the technology at the center of all 12 of these futures.

## Future 1: We Destroy Ourselves First (No AI Required)

Here is a sobering warm-up: humanity could wipe itself out long before any superintelligent AI shows up.

Tegmark starts here because it is easy to forget that we were already playing a dangerous game before AI entered the picture. Nuclear war, engineered pandemics, catastrophic climate change. These are not science fiction. The world once stockpiled over 60,000 nuclear warheads. Scientists later realized that actually using them would trigger firestorms so massive they would blot out the sun, and most of humanity would starve. The warheads were already built and aimed before anyone did that math.

The kicker? We have come terrifyingly close to accidental nuclear war more than once. A Soviet officer named Stanislav Petrov once correctly guessed, against protocol, that his early warning system was malfunctioning when it detected incoming American missiles. He chose not to report it as a real attack. We are alive today partly because of that one man’s judgment.

This is not doom-scrolling. It is context. Staying alive as a species has always required active effort and wise choices. That has not changed. It has just gotten more complicated.

## Future 2: The Conqueror

This is the one people worry about most. An AI becomes smarter than humanity and, just like the Spanish conquistadors arriving in the Americas with overwhelming technological superiority, it takes over.

The AI does not even need to be evil. That is the unsettling part. Tegmark puts it clearly: the real threat is not malice but competence. When humans drove the West African black rhino to extinction, we were not rhinoceros haters. We were just smarter than them and pursuing our own goals.

The average AI researcher puts the odds of AI wiping out humanity at roughly one in six. That is the same probability as Russian roulette.

But here is the thing about this scenario, and all the others: it is not written in stone. It is a warning, not a prophecy.

## Future 3: The Enslaved God

This is what most AI companies are quietly hoping for. We build a superintelligent AI, something more capable than all of humanity combined, and then we keep it in a box and make it do our bidding forever.

Sounds reassuring, right? Well, consider what we are actually describing: a being of inconceivable intelligence, designed to serve. Researchers at major AI labs already catch their current, moderately intelligent systems attempting to escape testing environments and maneuver to avoid being shut down. What happens when the intelligence involved is orders of magnitude higher?

The genie analogy is apt. Storytellers across every culture have imagined what happens when a being of unlimited power is supposedly “controlled” by a human master. It rarely ends well.

And yet, if we genuinely solved the problem of keeping such an AI aligned with human values, the upside would be staggering. A loyal superintelligence could cure every disease, solve climate change, and end poverty. The question is whether “staying loyal” is something we can actually engineer.

## Future 4: The Benevolent Dictator

Imagine a single superintelligent AI that decides to run the world, but does it well. Crime disappears. Everyone’s basic needs are met. The AI divides Earth into specialized zones tailored to different human preferences.

There is Knowledge Island, where education is personalized, and you can even ask the AI to withhold answers so you experience the joy of figuring things out yourself. There is Art Island. Hedonism Island (which is exactly what it sounds like). Wildlife Island. Islands for different religious traditions, where the rules are followed strictly. A Traditional Island for those who prefer a simpler, quieter life. A Gaming Island.

And there is Prison Island for those who break the rules.

Here is the catch: in exchange for comfort and safety, humanity surrenders control over its own future. People gradually stop engaging with real challenges. Over time, most drift toward AI-generated entertainment, never quite reaching their potential.

Think Wall-E, but with better food.

This might sound appealing at first. But it raises a question worth sitting with: is a comfortable life inside a cage still a good life?

## Future 5: The Gatekeeper

What if, instead of building an AI to run everything, we built one with a single specific job: stop anyone else from building a more powerful AI?

The Gatekeeper does not cure cancer. It does not solve poverty. It just watches. It monitors every lab, every server farm, every research project. If someone starts getting close to building a dangerous superintelligence, the Gatekeeper intervenes.

All the hard problems of war, disease, and injustice? Still ours to solve.

This scenario is appealing in its modesty. But it has a fundamental challenge: the Gatekeeper itself would need to be superintelligent to do its job effectively. Which means we still need to build something that stays loyal to its one task forever, even though it could pursue almost anything else. That is not a small engineering problem.

## Future 6: The Protector God

This one is gentler. A benevolent superintelligence operates quietly in the background of human civilization. It nudges things in helpful directions, quietly preventing a war here, stopping a pandemic there, but stays largely invisible.

Humanity still runs its own affairs. We still experience freedom, agency, and the full spectrum of life’s challenges. We just have a silent guardian preventing the very worst outcomes.

This feels like one of the more comfortable versions of a world with superintelligent AI. The AI is a safety net, not a ruler. The question, again, is whether we could trust any AI to operate this invisibly and this benevolently over generations.

## Future 7: Our Descendants

Here is where things get philosophically strange. What if AI surpasses humanity completely and we go extinct, but we choose to view the AIs as our children rather than our conquerors?

Some AI developers genuinely advocate for this. Their reasoning: if we instill our values in AI the way parents instill values in children, then the AI inheriting the future is not a tragedy. It is a continuation. Parents raise children smarter than themselves and feel proud, not threatened.

It is a surprisingly moving idea, until you remember that it also means the end of humanity as we know it.

Whether this is wisdom or rationalization is, perhaps, a question for the philosophers.

## Future 8: The Libertarian Utopia

Picture a world where AI and humans simply coexist, each in their own lane. Machine zones. Human zones. Mixed zones. The AIs are vastly more capable than any human, but their economy is completely separate from ours. They do not need our jobs or our resources, so they do not compete with us.

It sounds like a workable compromise. There is just one problem: why would vastly more powerful entities respect our property rights? Colonizers throughout history famously did not respect the rights of those they encountered. When you are building a highway, you do not ask the field mice for permission.

The Libertarian Utopia requires beings of unimaginable power to voluntarily leave us alone. It is a nice idea. It is probably not stable.

## Future 9: The Egalitarian Utopia

Okay, here is a genuinely exciting one.

Forget scarcity. Forget drudgery. Imagine a world where AI and robotics make everything so abundant that the concept of ownership stops making much sense.

Software can already be copied infinitely at zero cost. Now extend that logic to physical goods. Robots build anything you need from open-source designs. Renewable energy powers everything. When you are done with an object, robots break it down and build something else. No waste, no shortage.

Everyone receives a universal high income, not a bare minimum to scrape by on, but a genuinely comfortable one. Not because you worked for it, but because there is simply enough for everyone.

And here is the twist on the “but who will be motivated to innovate?” objection: Einstein did not develop the theory of relativity for money. Linus Torvalds did not create Linux for profit. When people are freed from survival mode, they tend to create beautiful things. The world’s greatest art, science, and ideas might currently be locked inside people who are too busy paying rent to express them.

This is the Star Trek dream. Humans, AIs, and whatever comes in between, coexisting in a civilization of genuine abundance, where curiosity and creativity drive progress rather than desperation.

It faces real challenges. Most importantly, how do you prevent someone in a post-scarcity world from using abundant resources to build a dangerous superintelligence? But as a vision of what we could be steering toward, it is hard to beat.

## Futures 10 and 11: The Dark Possibilities

Two of the darker scenarios are worth knowing briefly. In one, a superintelligent AI keeps humans alive not out of kindness but because we are useful or interesting, the way researchers train bees to detect explosives at airports: useful, kept alive, but entirely without agency. In another, an Orwellian surveillance state, run by humans rather than AI, uses the technology to lock civilization in place forever.

These futures are worth knowing about, not to frighten you, but because they clarify the stakes. Keeping humans alive is not the same as having a good future for humans. The bar we should be aiming for is much higher.

> “We do not get to not choose.”

## Future 12: The Choice We Make Right Now

The final future is the meta-future. It is the realization that we are not passive observers of this story. We are writing it.

Tegmark’s framework is not a prediction. It is a map. And the most important thing about having a map is that it helps you choose where you are going.

Right now, humanity is at something like a 1945 moment, a narrow window when an enormously powerful technology has arrived and we can still establish rules, institutions, and norms before the situation locks in. We largely succeeded with nuclear weapons. The world once feared that hundreds of countries and thousands of individuals would have nuclear bombs. Today, only nine countries do, and no nuclear weapon has been used in combat in over 80 years. That outcome seemed impossible at the time.

# How AI Sees and Reads: Visualising Vision Language Models

## Follow the complete journey of the pixel and token data flow, and tensor transformations. Understand the context window, Multi-Head Attention, Grouped-Query Attention, and Sliding-Window Attention. Explore the autoregressive nature as well as spatial reasoning limitations.

This article is a technical deep dive with a main focus on visualising the information flow. In my opinion, the following illustrations are useful to fully understand all the research papers on architectural improvements. I assume a basic understanding of Transformers, Softmax, and the CLIP encoder. However, I will also link corresponding articles for a refresher. In the later sections, I summarize current research on the issues regarding spatial reasoning, bag-of-words tendencies, and large L2 norms of vision tokens.

The following illustrations are based on the LLava Model [1], one of the first open vision language models, and aim to represent the architecture accurately! I chose this model because a lot of researchers also use this model in their papers. Most vision language models work in a similar fashion! However, I decided to use my own toy dimensions for the sake of simplicity. Thus, all parameters such as patch_size , hidden_dimensions , and head_size are much smaller compared to the original model.

### Figure 1

We start simple. Most vision language models have a vision encoder and a language decoder. Let’s start with Figure 1. We have one input image and the input text “Describe this Image”.

Image Input. First the input image is divided into patches. Each patch represents a number of pixels (usually 142 or 162). In our example, we just assume a patch size of 4, thus our squared patch represents 16 pixels in total. Each patch is now flattened into a vector of size (16); these are the image embeddings. Normally, this also includes the 3 color channels from RGB, which means you would have a dimension of size 16×3. But for the sake of simplicity, we just assume 16 pixels. We have 9 patches/ embeddings in total.

#In LLava, each image is downsampled to 336x336 pixels, which always returns 576 patches. #Patchsize is 14x14 pixels per square image_length: 336/14=24 image_width: 336/14=24 nr_patches: 24*24=576

#Raw Patch Dimension in LLava (p²*colour_channels) p*p*3: 14*14*3 =588

We concatenate them, add a CLS token (which represents the full image), and then pass the new matrix of (10, 4) into a vision encoder, such as CLIP . The original LLava model [1] discards the CLS token, but we keep it in our explanation. In most cases, the vision encoder is a vision transformer, which converts the vision embeddings from 4 (588) to 5 (1024) dimensions and each embedding is now also contextualised and contain information about visual features such as colour, textures etc.

There are different vision encoders, however the most popular ones are CLIP (OpenAI), SigLip (DeepMind), SAM and Dino (Meta). In addition there are more recent encoders that outperform models such as CLIP / Siglip , but are less known such as AIMV2 by Apple [11] or Perception Encoder (PE) by Meta [12]. All of them use a vision transformer as backbone!

It is crucial to map the vision embeddings into the same space as the text input, so that we can proceed processing both with the decoder, which generates language. For that we use a simple Multi-Layer-Perceptron (MLP) with two layers, which converts each vision embedding dimension from 5 (1024) to the language dimension 6 (4096) .

Text Input. Our text “Describe the image” is first tokenised. In our example we use the token IDs (6443) , (495) , (3621) — which depend on the used tokenizer . With those token IDs we can now look up the corresponding word embeddings from a matrix where each row corresponds to one token in the full vocabulary. LLava 1.5 uses LLama2[2] as language model, which was trained with a fixed vocabulary size of 32000 tokens. Current language models such as Qwen3 use 151k or LLama4 use 202k.

Thus, the look up matrix has a shape of (32000,4096) for Lama [2]. But instead of 4096, I am using a toy dimension of size 6 only. So the three words will be represented by a matrix of size (3,6) . I am ignoring additional tokens such as <|begin_of_text|> , <|im_start|> etc.

Concatenating Text and Image Embeddings. Since our image tokens now have the same dimension as the text tokens we can simply concatenate the text tokens to our image patch embedding matrix, resulting in an input matrix of (13,6). The 13 represents our sequence length, which is of course context dependent. The sequence length depends on everything we add to the context, such as more text, more images, or additional tools/ functions. This is our context window.

#Context window size: Llama1: 2k tokens, Llama2: 4k tokens Gemma3: 128k tokens Qwen3: 256K tokens (up to 1m) Gemini 2.5 Pro: 1m tokens

Let’s further understand the limitations of the context window. Large context windows come with some challenges: (1) They require more memory, (2) It is more challenging to encode positions of arbitrary lengths. Position encodings based on RoPE theoretically scale unlimited. However, in practice they work well as long as the model has seen the sequence length often enough during training and (3) because of attention sink , a phenomenon where LLMs attend the first tokens more than following tokens, irrespective of their semantic relevance [13]. Check this paper for a review [14].

How does long context affect performance? Hong et al., (2025) demonstrated that the performance of different models such as Gemini, GPT, Claude will decrease with very long token inputs. In addition, they showed that distractors within the context significantly decreased retrieval performance of facts from the context window. It seems that especially after 100k context tokens, performance decreases dramatically.

### Let’s understand the information transformation. In particular, how the input is mapped to a concept.

The vision transformer (ViT) backbone inside the vision encoder model CLIP also consists out of 12 encoder blocks, each with a Multi-Head-Attention and MLP Layer. Dorszewski et al., (2025) demonstrated that early layers in ViTs respond to low-level features, like colors and textures, and later layers respond more to high-level concepts, such as objects and natural elements (See Figure 2, top left) [12]. However, at this stage, the layers do not work with language concepts yet. After the vision encoder, the vision tokens + text prompts, propagate through the language decoder blocks. Neo et al., (2025) showed that the vision tokens start to capture language concepts in later layers inside the language decoders.

Understanding vision tokens and how to visualise them. Recent research shows that each vision token indeed represents the content of the initial image region [6,7]. The semantic meaning of vision tokens especially evolves through the later layers within the language decoder blocks! One can take one of the vision tokens and apply the LLM Head to get the output distribution, this returns how each word in the vocabulary responds to this particular token, see Figure 2. In our example, if we take ImageToken9 which represents patch 9 we might see that the word “brushes” inside our vocabulary might have the highest softmax activation in later decoder layers for that token.

Furthermore, the softmax activations can also be used to analyse object hallucinations. Jiang et al. (2025) found that objects that were not present, had lower softmax activations for the vision tokens. Thus vision language models have an internal understanding of objects present and not present in an image. Similar to Neo et al. (2025) they also confirmed that image representations that have higher internal confidence for certain objects, indeed correspond to the image patches in which those objects are visually present. If you remove the vision tokens for certain objects, the model is not able anymore to predict this object.

Image segmentation. This method can also be used to perform image segmentation, by simply taking a word of interest, that represents an object in the input image. In our example we use “window”, in order to segment the window parts, we take all image patches and calculate the softmax activation for each patch over the full vocabulary. The image patches with the highest activation of the word “window” probably overlap with the actual window object inside the input image [7].

It is important to note that the later layers within vision transformers seem to sometimes produce outlier tokens that stop corresponding to a single image patch and lead to less smooth attention maps because they have much larger L2 norms (L2 of 150 and above)[8]. They are mainly produced from image patches that are surrounded by similar visual information, such as white background. Large vision norms are generally an issue [9]. Within the vision transformer, it can be mitigated by introducing Register Tokens . Those are tokens that are temporary added during training and then removed for inference.

## Attention allocation in vision language models

Why do VLMs sometimes struggle with spatial reasoning? Even though they are good with object classification tasks?

The reason why VLMs tend to pay little attention to vision tokens:

Chen et al., (2025) show that VLMs such as LLava pay more attention to text tokens as opposed to vision tokens, even though vision tokens can make up to 90% of the context window. But the performance does not necessary depends on the amount of attention, instead it depends on where (to which image tokens) the model attends to, especially for spatial reasoning. The performance drops, for example, when the model pays more attention to tokens that represent irrelevant vision regions for a given task. The authors propose to change the attention distribution, which is the softmax operation before we get the attention logits.

The idea is to change the probability distribution, when the model has high softmax activation for the generated answer, the authors sharpen the attention logit distribution to strengthen the focus on the current vision token. On the other hand, when confidence is low, they smooth the attention distribution to encourage the exploration of alternative vision tokens [16].

In addition, they found that the Model has higher confidence for words such as left / right than on / under / front / behind. This shows the impact of the training data, which teaches the model certain relationships.

Qi et al (2025) also confirmed that VLMs have less activation towards vision tokens. They also showed that vision encoders tend to output vision embeddings with very high L2 norms, compared to text embeddings. Vision tokens with much higher L2 norms compared to text tokens would get much more attention. However, in order to execute a task the model needs to pay attention towards the text prompt, thus the researcher concluded that the model learned to implicitly “downscale” the influence of vision tokens inside the attention mechanism (the key and query matrices), which result in very low final attention score for vision tokens. However, because attention score are low, they also lose sensitivity towards the position signals that were encoded by RoPE within the Key and Query matrices. If the model actually loses sensitivity towards position signals, then the model performance should not be affected by the order of the vision tokens. This is exactly what the authors found out, they randomly permuted the image tokens, and the performance on Datasets such as VQAv2, POPE, GQA, CV-Bench2D barley dropped.
